notes:
# Psalm 124 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

**Title & Background.** The superscription reads "A Song of Ascents. Of David." Spurgeon notes that some "superfine critics" have challenged Davidic authorship based on alleged linguistic ornaments unknown in David's time, but he himself sees no reason to reject it: "the manner of the song is very like to David's" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php). Gill lists multiple possible historical settings: after David's conquest of the Philistines and Ammonites (2 Samuel 5:18), deliverance from Saul or Absalom, or even a prophetic anticipation of the return from Babylon (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm). Guzik notes that Boice favours a Davidic setting because the language of military attack fits better than captivity (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**Liturgical use in Reformed churches.** Ligonier notes that in many Reformed churches, verse 8 ("Our help is in the name of the LORD…") is used as the *votum* — the opening declaration of every worship service. "It is not a phrase to take lightly or to recite mechanically. It is an appropriate confession of God's people as they start a week" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/preserved-through-pilgrimage).

---

## v. 1 — "If the LORD had not been on our side— let Israel now declare—"

**The abrupt opening.** Spurgeon describes the opening as "abrupt, and remains a fragment" — a burst of poetic fire that arrests attention. He suggests the literal sense is: "Had it not been Jehovah! He was for us, oh let Israel say!" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php). Bellarmine (cited in Spurgeon) says such unfinished expressions "indicate the great joy and exultation that will not suffer the speaker to finish his sentences."

**"On our side."** Guzik draws on VanGemeren: the Hebrew phrase *hayah lanu* is "the past tense of Immanuel ('God is with us'). Thus the community confesses that God has been with them in their past history." Meyer adds: "Here is an If which cannot be an if. It is never a matter of uncertainty whether the Lord will be on our side or not" — for Christ in His incarnation and death has taken His place beside us forevermore (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**Gill's Trinitarian reading.** Gill expounds "on our side" in a distinctively Trinitarian way: God the Father is on our side by His love and relation to us; Christ is on our side as Surety, Saviour, Captain, Advocate, and interceding High Priest; the Spirit is on our side to carry on His work in us, assist us in prayer, secure us from Satan's temptations, and bring us safe to heaven (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm).

**"Let Israel now say."** Guzik emphasises that David thought it necessary for *all* God's covenant people — not just a few — to declare this publicly. "It was the duty of all Israel to know and to say that God was their absolutely essential help" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

---

## v. 2 — "if the LORD had not been on our side when men attacked us"

**The repetition.** Luther (cited in both Spurgeon and Guzik) explains the repetition pastorally: "Whilst we are in danger, our fear is without measure; but when it is once past, we imagine it to have been less than it was indeed. And this is the delusion of Satan, to diminish and obscure the grace of God. David therefore with this repetition stirreth up the people to more thankfulness" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

**"When men rose up against us."** Guzik identifies the most likely occasion as the Philistine threat at the start of David's reign (2 Samuel 5:17–25). Kidner is cited: "As a psalm of David, this gives us a rare insight into the early peril of his kingdom, particularly from the Philistines" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/). Spurgeon widens it: "When all men combined, and the whole race of men seemed set upon stamping out the house of Israel… No one who could or would help was near, but the bare arm of the Lord sufficed" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php). Gill notes that the enemies are called merely "men" — "though no hard epithet is given in the text, however just" — displaying the meekness of God's people (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm). Daniel Dyke (in Spurgeon) adds: the enemies, though "monsters rather than men," are called "men" because the church "would leave the further censuring of them unto God their righteous Judge" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

---

## v. 3 — "then they would have swallowed us alive, when their anger flared against us"

**Swallowed alive.** Spurgeon says the enemies "would have made only one morsel of us, and have swallowed us up alive and whole in a single instant." He draws the moral: "The cruel world would make a full end of the godly seed were it not that Jehovah bars the way" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php). Ellicott's Commentary notes an allusion to the fall of Korah (Numbers 16:32–33), where the same Hebrew verb and adjective for "swallowed alive" occur together (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/124.htm, via search excerpt). Cresswell (in Spurgeon) adds that the image may also refer to a man shut up alive in a sepulchre (Proverbs 1:12) or swallowed by an earthquake (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

**"Their anger flared / wrath was kindled."** Spurgeon: "Anger is never more fiery than when the people of God are its objects. Sparks become flames, and the furnace is heated seven times hotter when God's elect are to be thrust into the blaze" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php; also cited by Guzik at https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**Maclaren's emphasis.** Guzik quotes Maclaren: "One thought runs through it all, that the sole actor in their deliverance has been Jehovah. No human arm has been bared for them; no created might could have rescued them" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

---

## vv. 4–5 — "then the floods would have engulfed us, then the torrent would have overwhelmed us, then the raging waters would have swept us away"

**The flood imagery.** Spurgeon unpacks the transition from beast to water imagery: "Rising irresistibly, like the Nile, the flood of opposition would soon have rolled over our heads." He distinguishes the "steadily rising flood" (v. 4a) from the "hurriedly rushing stream" (v. 4b). "Who can stand against two such mighty powers? Everything is destroyed by these unconquerable forces, either by being submerged or swept away" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

**"The stream had gone over our soul."** Spurgeon: "The rushing torrent would have drowned our soul, our hope, our life." Guzik notes the repetition of "gone over our soul" (vv. 4 and 5) emphasises that the danger was "not only political or economic; it had to do with the very soul, with life at the deepest levels" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**"Proud waters" (v. 5).** Spurgeon: the waves are pictured as proud, "and so they seem to be when they overleap the bulwarks of a frail bark." He applies this to persecution: "The opposition of men is usually embittered by a haughty scorn which derides all our godly efforts as mere fanaticism or obstinate ignorance." The Expositor's Bible Commentary notes that the rare Hebrew word rendered "proud" comes from a root meaning "to boil over" and may apply "rather to the persons signified by the waters than to the flood itself" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-124.html, via search excerpt). Gill interprets the proud waters simply as "the wicked, who, through their pride, persecute the poor saints" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm).

**Reformed perspective.** Ligonier ties the flood imagery to the whole history of God's outnumbered people: "Picture enormous armies of powerful, hate-filled, and predatory foes. Israel seems to have no chance against the armies of Egyptians or Assyrians… The psalmist uses enemies as a foil to highlight the power and care of the Lord" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-help-is-in-the-name-of-the-lord).

---

## v. 6 — "Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth"

**"Blessed be the LORD."** Guzik explains this is not bestowing a blessing on Yahweh but "thanking, praising, and announcing Him as blessed" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/). Spurgeon: "It implies that none can harm us till the Lord permits: we cannot be their prey unless the Lord gives us up to them, and that our loving Lord will never do" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

**"Prey to their teeth."** Kidner (cited by Guzik) notes this is "not quite the same figure as that of Psalm 124:3. In these jaws we feel the slower agonies of defeat, like the tearing and grinding of the prey." The picture shifts from the sudden swallowing of verse 3 to a prolonged, grinding destruction (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**Gill.** Gill ties the "teeth" imagery to Psalm 57:4 ("their teeth are spears and arrows") and 1 Peter 5:8 (Satan as a devouring lion). God will not give His people up as prey, "nay, when they have seized them, and got them in their mouths, they shall be snatched from them, as the lamb out of the mouth of the lion and the bear by David" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm).

**Ligonier.** Ligonier describes verse 6 as a picture of the Lord plucking Israel away "from the jaws of the enemy" — a vivid image of last-second deliverance (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-help-is-in-the-name-of-the-lord).

---

## v. 7 — "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler; the net is torn, and we have slipped away"

**The bird and the snare.** This is the most commented-upon image in the psalm.

*Maclaren* (cited by Guzik): "The comparison of the soul to a bird is beautiful [cf. Psalm 11:1]. It hints at tremors and feebleness, at alternations of feeling like the flutter of some weak-winged songster, at the utter helplessness of the panting creature in the toils" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/). The Expositor's Bible Commentary adds: "One hand only could break the snare, and then the bruised wings were swiftly spread for flight once more, and up into the blue went the ransomed joy, with a song instead of harsh notes of alarm" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-124.html, via search excerpt).

*Spurgeon* provides an extensive meditation on the fowler as Satan: "Fowlers have many methods of taking small birds, and Satan has many methods of entrapping souls. Some are decoyed by evil companions, others are enticed by the love of dainties; hunger drives many into the trap, and fright impels numbers to fly into the net." He then applies it evangelistically: "Hear this, ye that are slaves to drunkenness: God can deliver you. You that have fallen into licentiousness hear it – God can deliver you. Whatever the sin that has birdlimed [trapped] you, that gracious hand which once was nailed to the cross can set you free" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php; also https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**"The snare is broken, and we are escaped."** Spurgeon notes the deliberate repetition: "The song is worth repeating; it is well to dwell upon so great a mercy." He lists possible snares: "false doctrine, pride, lust, or a temptation to indulge in policy, or to despair, or to presume." The mercy is often unrecognised while we are still in the snare; "the gratitude comes when the escape is seen" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

**The snare's mechanism (Reformed).** Ligonier provides a historical detail: one type of fowler's snare was "a lightweight circular net with weights around the edges. They would cast it over a flock of small birds." The deliverance is "a picture of an unlikely event and an unusual last-second providence. Just at the moment when everything seemed over, the Lord delivered His people" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-help-is-in-the-name-of-the-lord).

**Gill's application.** Gill identifies the fowlers as "Satan, and wicked men under his influence, who lay snares… to draw them into sin, into immorality and error." The breaking of the snare means "measures concerted by wicked men are broken, their schemes are confounded, their devices are disappointed" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm).

**Resurrection hope (Reformed).** Ligonier extends the escaped-bird image to the ultimate deliverance: "It reminds us ultimately, however, of the hope of the resurrection: even death and the grave cannot entrap a believer. Death no longer has dominion over us" (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-help-is-in-the-name-of-the-lord).

---

## v. 8 — "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth"

**Defiance and confidence.** Guzik: "We sense a bit of defiance in this declaration. The nations find their supposed help in their supposed deities; God's people confidently find their help in the name of the LORD" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/). Spurgeon: "Our Creator is our preserver… Did he create all that we see, and can he not preserve us from evils which we cannot see?" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

**The name.** Spurgeon says "Jehovah's revealed character is our foundation of confidence, his person is our sure fountain of strength." Gill ties "the name of the Lord" to the Messiah: "in the Messiah; in whom the name of the Lord is, his nature and perfections; and in whom help is found" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm).

**Trapp** (cited by Guzik): "Experience should breed confidence… write up experiences therefore, oft rub them over, and then conclude as here" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**Edersheim's "threefold cord"** (cited in Spurgeon): These three things I will bear on my heart, O Lord: "The Lord was on our side," this for the past; "The snare is broken," for the present; "Our help is in the name of the Lord," this for the future. "I will not and I cannot be fainthearted… so long as I hold this 'threefold cord' in my hand, or rather, am held by it" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php).

**Reformed votum.** As noted above, many Reformed churches open every worship service with this verse as the *votum* (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/preserved-through-pilgrimage).

---

## Traditions Compared

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill).** The Baptist reading, epitomised by Spurgeon, is strongly experiential and evangelistic. Spurgeon reads the "if" as a spur to personal testimony, the flood as the combined forces of "earth and hell," and the snare as personal sin from which the cross of Christ alone can free us. Gill adds a thorough Trinitarian framework to verse 1 and reads "the name of the Lord" in verse 8 as pointing to the Messiah. The emphasis falls on the individual believer's deliverance from sin and Satan. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm)

**Reformed (Ligonier).** The Reformed reading emphasises God's sovereign providence over history: the psalm reflects the pattern of God's people always being the outnumbered minority, with enemies used as a foil "to highlight the power and care of the Lord." Deliverance is "an unusual last-second providence." The ultimate horizon is the resurrection — death itself cannot entrap the believer. The liturgical use of verse 8 as the *votum* is a distinctive Reformed practice. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-help-is-in-the-name-of-the-lord; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/preserved-through-pilgrimage)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik).** Guzik's commentary (used widely in Pentecostal and charismatic circles) emphasises the repeated phrase "gone over our soul" as teaching that troubles attack "the very soul, with life at the deepest levels." He identifies multiple categories of soul-trouble: being swallowed, overwhelmed, swept away, ground to powder, and trapped. The repeated emphasis on the soul — not just external circumstances — reflects a charismatic concern with inner spiritual life. The snare-breaking is applied to freedom from besetting sins and bondages. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/)

**Pulpit Commentary / Homiletics.** The Pulpit Commentary takes a broader redemptive-historical approach: the psalm is "the language of Israel's gratitude," then "that of redeemed humanity," then "that of the Church of God" throughout her history of persecution. It makes the striking point that "God is on our side when He seems most against us — as He was on the side of the Israelites both in delivering them over to the Captivity and in breaking their bonds. Punishment and pardon have the same end in view — the redemption of the sinner" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/124.htm, via search excerpt).

**Ellicott (Anglican).** Ellicott's Commentary takes a critical-historical approach: the psalm reflects nothing less than "the total ruin of the city and Temple, and the captivity of the nation." He sees the older Exodus deliverance as colouring the language, and notes that "the Aramaisms of the poem leave no room for upholding the ascription to David." The rhythm is described as "finely varied" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/124.htm, via search excerpt). This represents the older Anglican scholarly tradition that was open to critical questions about authorship.

**The Expositor's Bible Commentary.** This commentary also favours a post-exilic setting: "This psalm is an outgush of the first rapture of astonishment and joy for deliverance so sudden and complete. It is most naturally taken as the expression of the feelings of the exiles on their restoration from Babylon." The dominant note is that "the sole actor in their deliverance has been Jehovah" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-124.html, via search excerpt).

---

## Other Views

**Historical use in Scotland (1582).** Both Spurgeon and Guzik record the famous event in Edinburgh where an imprisoned minister, John Durie, was freed and met by a crowd that grew to 2,000, who sang Psalm 124 in four-part harmony up the High Street. One persecutor "is said to have been more alarmed at this sight and song than at anything he had seen in Scotland" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps124.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-124/).

**Gill's catalogue of historical settings.** Gill lists the full range of traditional identifications: the Red Sea deliverance, David's wars, the return from Babylon, and the Maccabean crisis. He concludes it "may be applied to any time of distress the church and people of God have been in" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/124.htm).
